question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
answer: No. When a creature phases back in ('phases in'), that is not treated as it entering the battlefield, so "enters the battlefield" (ETB) triggered abilities do not trigger. Rule [702.26d] states explicitly that phasing doesn't actually cause a permanent to change zones or control, and that 'Zone-change triggers don't trigger when a permanent phases in or out.' Since ETB abilities are a type of zone-change trigger (as defined in [603.6a]), a phased-in creature's own ETB ability, and any other permanent's 'whenever a creature enters' ability, will not fire when a creature phases back in. Similarly, attachment triggers (like 'whenever this becomes attached') also don't fire on phasing per [702.26j], for the same underlying reason: phasing is not treated as a real zone or control change, just a temporary change of status (phased in/phased out) as described in [110.5b] and [702.26b]/[702.26c]. This holds whether the phasing happens via the normal untap-step turn-based action ([502.1], [703.4a], [702.26a]) or via a 'phases out until...' effect ([610.4], [610.4a], [610.4c]) — in all these cases the permanent never actually left the battlefield, it was merely treated as though it didn't exist while phased out, so its return isn't an entrance.

Zone-change triggers don’t trigger when a permanent phases in or out. Tokens continue to exist on the battlefield while phased out. Counters and stickers remain on a permanent while it’s phased out. Effects that check a phased-in permanent’s history won’t treat the phasing event as having caused the permanent to leave or enter the battlefield or its controller’s control.

question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
answer:
When a creature has both trample and deathtouch, deathtouch changes what counts as "lethal damage" for the trample-assignment rules, letting the attacker send far less damage to blockers and much more to the defending player (or planeswalker/battle).

Normally, trample (rule 702.19b) requires the attacking creature's controller to assign at least lethal damage to each blocking creature before any excess can go to the player, planeswalker, or battle it's attacking. "Lethal damage" is normally damage equal to or greater than the blocker's toughness (see the Lethal Damage definition, rules 120.4a and 302.7/704.5g). But rule 702.2c states that any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered lethal damage for the purpose of determining excess damage. So if the attacking creature has deathtouch, the controller only needs to assign 1 damage to each blocking creature to satisfy the 'lethal damage' requirement of trample (rule 702.19b) — the rest can be assigned to the defending player, planeswalker, or battle as excess.

Example: a 5/5 creature with trample and deathtouch is blocked by a 4/4 creature with no abilities. Normally the attacker would need to assign at least 4 damage to the blocker before trampling over. With deathtouch, the attacker's controller only needs to assign 1 damage to the blocking creature (which is treated as lethal per 702.2c), and can assign the remaining 4 damage to the defending player. That 1 damage marked on the blocking creature will also cause it to be destroyed as a state-based action once damage is dealt, per rule 702.2b/704.5h, regardless of its toughness, since it was dealt by a deathtouch source.

The same principle applies to trample over planeswalkers (rule 702.19c): once 1 damage (lethal, thanks to deathtouch) has been assigned to each blocker, and damage at least equal to the planeswalker's loyalty has been assigned to it, remaining damage can go to the blockers, the planeswalker, or the planeswalker's controller. Deathtouch doesn't reduce the amount needed against the planeswalker itself — deathtouch's 'any nonzero amount is lethal' rule only applies to creatures, not to loyalty on planeswalkers or defense on battles (rule 120.4a distinguishes creatures, planeswalkers, and battles for this purpose).

This analysis is the same whether there are two players or more than two, since these rules concern damage assignment to blockers and to whichever player, planeswalker, or battle is being attacked — nothing about deathtouch/trample assignment changes with additional players at the table.

When checking for assigned lethal damage, take into account damage already marked on the creature and damage from other creatures that’s being assigned during the same combat damage step, but not any abilities or effects that might change the amount of damage that’s actually dealt. question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
answer:
Yes—Storm is a triggered ability, and like other triggered abilities it can be countered, but only by an effect that specifically says it counters abilities (not by something that "counters only spells").

Rule 702.40a defines Storm as a triggered ability that functions on the stack: "When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn..." Because it's a triggered ability rather than a spell, once it's on the stack (per 603.3/603.3d, put there the next time a player would receive priority) it is governed by rule 113.9: "Activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren't spells, and therefore can't be countered by anything that counters only spells. Activated and triggered abilities on the stack can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities." Static abilities, by contrast, don't use the stack and can never be countered, but that's not relevant here since Storm is explicitly triggered, not static.

So if an opponent has an effect like "counter target spell," that cannot stop the Storm trigger itself (though it could of course counter the Storm-carrying spell before the trigger even fires, or counter the copies once they're spells on the stack). Only an effect worded to counter an ability (e.g., "counter target activated or triggered ability") can counter the Storm trigger itself.

question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
answer:
No — a card with a hybrid mana symbol counts as being every color shown in that symbol, so it can only go in a commander deck whose commander's color identity includes ALL of those colors, not just one of them. Rule [202.2d] and [107.4e] both state that a hybrid mana symbol (such as {R/G}) makes the object all of the colors of its components — {R/G}{R/G} is red AND green, even though you could pay it with any mix of red/green mana. Because of this, rule [903.4f] (color identity) counts every color in a hybrid symbol as part of that card's color identity. Rule [903.5c] then requires that every color in a card's color identity be found in the color identity of the deck's commander for that card to be legal in the deck. So if your commander is, say, mono-red, a card containing {R/G} or {W/R} hybrid symbols is illegal in that deck, because green (or white) isn't part of the commander's color identity — even though you'd never actually be forced to spend green mana to cast it. The fact that hybrid mana can be *paid* with either color (per rule [118.13] and the payment mechanics in [106.8]/[118.7e]) doesn't change what colors the card *is* for deck-construction purposes; color identity looks at the symbols printed on the card, not how you choose to pay for it. The only way a hybrid card is legal with a single-color commander is if the commander's color identity happens to include both halves of every hybrid symbol on that card (as with Wort, the Raidmother, whose red-green identity per [903.5c] and [903.5d] would let in a red/green hybrid card, but not a card with, say, {U/B} hybrid symbols).

This is a Commander-specific deckbuilding rule; the provided rules context doesn't include multiplayer-specific exceptions to this particular restriction, so the answer is the same regardless of player count — color identity and the 903.5c requirement apply table-wide, not per-opponent.

question: can I respond to the untap step?
answer:
No. During the untap step, no player receives priority at all, so you cannot cast spells, activate abilities, or otherwise "respond" to anything that happens there. Rule [502.4] states this directly: "No player receives priority during the untap step. Any ability that triggers during this step will be held until the next time a player would receive priority, which is usually during the upkeep step." This is reinforced by [117.3a], which lists the untap step as one of the times no player gets priority, and by [500.3], which notes the untap step is one of only a couple of steps where no player receives priority at all (the other being certain cleanup steps, per [514.3]).

What actually happens during the untap step is a set of turn-based actions, not spells or abilities: phased-in permanents the active player controls phase out and permanents they controlled when they phased out phase in ([502.1], [703.4a]), the day/night designation is checked ([731.2]), and then the active player untaps the permanents they choose to untap, all simultaneously ([703.4c]). Turn-based actions like these don't use the stack ([703.1], [502.1], [514.1] gives another example of a turn-based action not using the stack).

If something triggers during the untap step (for example, an ability that triggers "whenever a permanent phases in"), that triggered ability doesn't go on the stack immediately — it's held and put onto the stack the next time a player would receive priority, which is usually at the start of the upkeep step, before the active player gets priority there ([502.4], [503.1a]). So effectively, you get your first chance to respond to anything connected to the untap step once the upkeep step begins.

This holds true regardless of how many players are in the game — nothing in the untap step rules changes based on player count, and no multiplayer-specific rule here alters priority timing during untap.

question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
answer:
Yes. A creature that declared as an attacker (or was put onto the battlefield attacking) remains an "attacking creature" until it is removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever happens first [508.1k, Attacking Creature]. The end of combat step is the fifth and final step of the combat phase, not a separate phase [511.1, End of Combat Step], so simply reaching or being in the end of combat step does not end the combat phase and does not by itself remove creatures from combat. The combat phase itself doesn't end until the end of combat step is over: "As soon as the end of combat step ends, all creatures, battles, and planeswalkers are removed from combat. question: Do you cast lands?
answer:
No. You never "cast" a land card—you "play" it. Playing a land is one of the special actions defined in the rules (rule [116.2a]), and it doesn't use the stack at all. A player who has priority may play a land card from their hand during a main phase of their own turn, once per turn (barring effects granting extra land plays), only when the stack is empty [305.1] [505.6b] [701.18a]. Because the land never goes on the stack, it is never a spell, and no one can respond to it with instants or activated abilities [305.1] [505.6b].

By contrast, "casting" is the specific process (defined in rule 601, "Casting Spells") used for spells like creatures, instants, sorceries, etc.—for example, casting a creature card does use the stack [302.1]. Historically some old card text used "play" to mean "cast," but that wording has been updated via Oracle errata to say "cast" instead [601.1] [601.1a]. The general term "play a card" can mean either playing it as a land or casting it as a spell, whichever is appropriate for that card [701.18b] [601.1a].

A couple of related points: if a permanent is both a land and another card type (like an artifact land), it can only ever be played as a land, never cast as a spell [305.9] [300.2a]. Also, lands are played without paying any cost, and most land cards simply have no mana cost printed on them at all [202.1b]. Finally, if an effect merely lets you "put" a land onto the battlefield (rather than "play" it), that's not the same as playing a land and doesn't use your one land-play for the turn [305.4].

This holds the same whether you're in a two-player or multiplayer game—rule 305.3 simply requires that it be your own turn to play a land, regardless of how many players are at the table.

question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
answer:
Yes. After an evoked creature enters the battlefield, its evoke triggered ability ("When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it," per rule 702.74a) is put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority (603.3d), not immediately. Since the ability sits on the stack waiting to resolve, and rule 608.1 tells us a spell or ability only resolves once all players pass priority in succession, there is a window where players have priority before that trigger resolves. During that window you (or anyone else, depending on the effect) can respond by activating some other sacrifice outlet (an activated ability, another spell, etc.) and sacrifice the evoked creature yourself, since it is already a permanent on the battlefield and thus a legal sacrifice target for such an effect.

If you do sacrifice the creature that way before the evoke trigger resolves, then when the evoke trigger finally resolves it will find that the permanent it's supposed to sacrifice is no longer on the battlefield. A triggered ability's source and referenced objects use last-known information only for things like determining characteristics for the effect (rule 113.7a), but you can't actually 'sacrifice' an object that no longer exists in the zone it needs to be sacrificed from — sacrificing requires moving the permanent from the battlefield to the graveyard, which is impossible if it's already gone. So the evoke trigger simply does nothing further in that case; you don't get sacrificed 'twice' or suffer any extra effect, and the earlier sacrifice (from whatever other ability you used) is what actually got the creature into the graveyard.

Note this is different from trying to use the evoke trigger itself to sacrifice the creature 'early' — that specific triggered ability only does its sacrifice when it resolves (608.1). What you're describing is using a separate, independent sacrifice effect in the meantime, which is legal because priority is passed around before the evoke trigger resolves.

question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
answer:
Yes. Keyword abilities are abilities like any other, so an effect that says a permanent "loses all abilities" strips away all of its keyword abilities (flying, trample, deathtouch, etc.) along with any other granted or printed abilities.

According to rule [702.1], a keyword such as "flying" or "trample" is just a shorthand name for an ability that could otherwise be spelled out in full rules text — the reminder text merely summarizes the underlying game rule, but the keyword itself represents a genuine ability. Rule [113.10] and [113.10b] establish that "loses that ability" (or "loses all abilities") removes abilities, and such removal effects "remove all instances" of the specified ability/abilities — there's no carve-out for keywords versus spelled-out abilities.

One important caveat from rule [113.12]: this only removes actual granted/printed *abilities*. If something is instead a defined characteristic (e.g., "this creature is red") or a stated quality (e.g., "this creature can't be blocked") rather than a keyword or written ability, a "loses all abilities" effect does not touch it, because those aren't abilities in the rules sense. Likewise, characteristic-defining abilities under rule [604.3] convey characteristics like power/toughness or color, but they are still technically abilities, so a "loses all abilities" effect would strip those too unless something else is protecting them.

This reasoning doesn't depend on whether it's a two-player or multiplayer game — the ability-removal mechanics work the same regardless of player count.

question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
answer:
Yes. Your maximum hand size doesn't stop you from drawing cards at any point during the game - it only matters at cleanup. You can draw as many cards as an effect instructs, even while already above your maximum hand size (normally seven, or six if you're using a vanguard card with a -1 hand modifier, as in [313.6] and [902.5b]).

According to [402.2], "a player may have any number of cards in their hand," and the maximum hand size only forces a discard "as part of their cleanup step." The actual turn-based action that enforces this is described in [514.1] and [703.4n]: immediately after the cleanup step begins, if the active player's hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size, they discard down to that number. This is a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack, and it only happens during the cleanup step - not whenever you draw.

So if you draw a card (or several) while already at or above your maximum hand size, the draw(s) happen normally. You'll simply be over your maximum hand size until your next cleanup step, at which point you'll need to discard down to your maximum (e.g., to seven, or to six under a vanguard card's -1 modifier per [902.5b]).

One caveat: if your library runs out of cards and you're required to draw, you draw whatever remains and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority, per [104.3c] - that's a separate issue from hand size and applies regardless of how many cards are in your hand.

question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
answer:
A planeswalker with 0 loyalty counters is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action. This happens automatically the next time state-based actions are checked (which occurs before any player would receive priority) — no player needs to do anything, and it doesn't use the stack.

Some background on why this matters: loyalty is a characteristic only planeswalkers have, and it's tracked by loyalty counters placed on the permanent — the planeswalker's loyalty equals the number of loyalty counters on it [306.5c]. A planeswalker enters the battlefield with a number of loyalty counters equal to its printed loyalty number, via a replacement effect [306.5b][614.1c]. Damage dealt to a planeswalker doesn't reduce its life or destroy it directly — instead, it causes that many loyalty counters to be removed from the planeswalker [306.8][120.3c]. Loyalty counters can also be removed by activating loyalty abilities or by other effects.

Once a planeswalker's loyalty counters are removed down to 0 (note: loyalty can't meaningfully go 'below' zero since it's just a count of counters, so 'zero or less' in practice just means zero), the game's state-based actions notice this and put that planeswalker into its owner's graveyard [306.9][122.1e][704.5i]. State-based actions are checked automatically and continuously whenever a player would receive priority [704.1], so this happens essentially immediately after the loyalty hits 0, without needing a spell or ability to explicitly cause it.

This is analogous to how a player with 0 or less life loses the game as a state-based action [119.6][104.3b], or how a battle with 0 defense is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action [310.7] — all are SBAs that police these counters/values automatically.

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players at the table; the graveyard-placement rule for a 0-loyalty planeswalker applies the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: do non-creature artifacts die?
answer: No. In Magic's rules terminology, only creatures and planeswalkers can "die" — the glossary entry [Dies] states: "A creature or planeswalker 'dies' if it is put into a graveyard from the battlefield," and rule [700.4] defines the general term "dies" the same way ("is put into a graveyard from the battlefield") but that terminology is only applied to creatures and planeswalkers in practice. A non-creature artifact that goes from the battlefield to its owner's graveyard has indeed been "put into a graveyard from the battlefield," but that event is not called "dying" for an artifact — it's just going to the graveyard (whether via being destroyed, sacrificed, or some other effect). This matters for triggered abilities: an ability that says "Whenever a creature dies..." would not trigger off a non-creature artifact going to the graveyard, because that artifact never "died" — it just left the battlefield. Note that an artifact creature (an artifact that is also a creature) *would* die when put into a graveyard from the battlefield, since it satisfies the creature condition in the [Dies] definition. question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
answer:
You don't lose immediately — you lose the game the next time any player would receive priority, as a state-based action. Attempting to draw from an empty library doesn't crash the game or fizzle silently; the game notes that you tried to draw with no cards left, and then the loss is applied as a state-based action.

Specifically: drawing a card means putting the top card of your library into your hand [Draw]. If your library has no cards and you're required to draw (whether it's the normal turn-based draw in your draw step [504.1], or a draw from a spell/ability [121.1]), you simply can't produce a card — but the attempt itself is what matters. Rule [121.4] and [704.5b] say that a player who attempted to draw from an empty library loses the game the next time a state-based action check happens and a player would receive priority, not the instant the draw fails. If you were required to draw *more cards than remain* (e.g., library has 2 cards but you must draw 5), rule [104.3c] says you draw the cards that are actually there, and then lose under the same state-based-action timing.

This is a state-based action per the general framework in [704.1], so it's checked continuously, but the actual game-loss doesn't take effect until priority is about to be given to someone — there's a brief window where the failed draw has happened but the loss hasn't been applied yet, during which triggered abilities from the draw attempt (if any) would still go on the stack.

A few related wrinkles: if an effect merely *offers you the choice* to draw while your library is empty, you can still choose to do so per [121.3]/[121.3a] — it just won't produce a card and will trigger the same losing state-based action. If an effect *replaces* the draw entirely, that replacement effect still applies even though there are no cards to draw, per [121.6a] and [614.11], meaning you may not lose at all because you never "attempted to draw" in the normal sense — the draw was replaced by something else. Also, moving cards to your hand from your library without using the word "draw" isn't a draw at all [121.5], so an empty library in that case doesn't trigger this losing condition.

This all applies the same way whether you're in a two-player game or a multiplayer game — the losing condition is tied to that individual player's empty library and the draw attempt, not to turn order or number of opponents, so nothing in the provided rules suggests a different outcome in multiplayer.

question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
answer:
The combat phase has five steps, in order: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat (rule 506.1). If no creatures are declared as attackers (or put onto the battlefield attacking), the declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped entirely (rule 508.8). If any attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike, there are two combat damage steps instead of one (rule 506.1).

As the defending player, you get priority in each step after the active player has had priority and passed it to you. Priority itself works like this: the active player receives priority at the beginning of most steps and phases, but only after any turn-based actions for that step (like drawing a card, or in the beginning of combat step, determining the defending player) have been completed and any triggered abilities have been put on the stack (rule 117.3a). Turn-based actions themselves don't involve priority at all — for example, choosing the defending player at the start of the beginning of combat step (rules 507.1, 703.4h) and the assignment/dealing of combat damage in the combat damage step (rules 510.1, 510.2, 703.4k) all happen without anyone having priority. Once those turn-based actions are done, the active player gets priority; if the active player passes priority without doing anything, priority passes to you as the defending (nonactive) player, and you can then cast spells or activate abilities (rule 117.1). This 'active player first, then you' pattern is illustrated directly in rule 732.2b, where a nonactive player is shown holding priority during the beginning of combat step only after the active player has passed. The end of combat step has no turn-based actions at all, so the active player simply gets priority as soon as the step begins (rule 511.1), and you'd get priority after the active player passes.

This description (one defending player who gets priority after the active/attacking player in each step) is accurate for a two-player game (rule 506.2a). In a multiplayer game the picture can differ: there may be one or more defending players depending on the variant (rule 506.2). If the 'attack multiple players' option is in use, all of the attacking player's opponents automatically become defending players (rule 802.2) rather than the attacking player choosing just one. Otherwise, the active player chooses one opponent as the defending player as a turn-based action during the beginning of combat step (rules 507.1, 703.4h). When there are multiple defending players, combat damage assignment during the combat damage step is done in APNAP (active-player, then non-active-players in turn order) order rather than by a single defending player (rules 802.5, 703.4k). The Shared Team Turns variant changes this further, having the active team announce attacker damage assignment and the defending team announce blocker damage assignment (rule 805.10f).

question: can i respond to a mana ability?
answer:
No. Mana abilities never go on the stack, so they resolve immediately and can't be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. This is true whether the mana ability is activated (like tapping a land) or triggered.

Rule 113.4 establishes that mana abilities "don't use the stack, and, under certain circumstances, a player can activate mana abilities even if they don't have priority." For activated mana abilities specifically, rule 605.3b says: "An activated mana ability doesn't go on the stack, so it can't be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. Rather, it resolves immediately after it is activated." This is echoed in 405.6c, which notes that mana abilities resolve immediately, and if a player had priority before activating one, they get priority back right after it resolves — no window opens for anyone else to act in between.

Triggered mana abilities work the same way: rule 605.4a says a triggered mana ability "doesn't go on the stack, so it can't be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. Rather, it resolves immediately after the mana ability that triggered it, without waiting for priority."

One nuance: a permanent's ability only counts as a mana ability if it meets the criteria in 605.1a/605.1b (no target, could produce mana, not a loyalty ability). If an ability has a target, or is a spell (which per 605.5b can never be a mana ability), it's not a mana ability at all — it uses the stack normally and can be responded to.

This holds true regardless of player count — nothing in these rules changes based on whether it's a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since mana abilities bypass the stack and priority system entirely rather than going through turn-order-dependent priority passing.

question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
answer:
No. Paying a cost is not something you get to respond to with a spell or ability of your own—it's an internal step within a single, all-or-nothing process (casting a spell, activating an ability, or the turn-based actions of declaring attackers/blockers), and none of those processes use the stack or pass priority until the whole process is finished.

When a spell is cast, the total cost is determined and then "locked in" (rule 601.2f), and payment of that cost is completed as part of steps 601.2f–h before any player receives priority. The only thing you get to do mid-payment is activate your own mana abilities to help pay a mana cost (rule 118.2, rule 601.2g), and that's not a response to the cost being paid—it's part of paying it. Once that resulting total cost is locked in, no effect can change it further (rule 601.2f), and activating a cost-altering ability afterward has no effect on the spell or ability already on the stack (rule 602.4).

The same is true for declaring attackers and declaring blockers: these are turn-based actions that don't use the stack (rule 508.1i, rule 508.1j, rule 509.1e, rule 509.1f). Any mana abilities needed for costs (like a 'convoke' or 'kicker' cost involving mana, or an ability that requires mana to attack/block) are activated as part of that same turn-based action, and the declaration is either completed legally in full or, if a cost can't be paid, the entire declaration is treated as illegal and reversed per rule 733.1 (partial payments aren't allowed, per 508.1i/j and 509.1e/f).

So in every case, 'paying a cost' is atomic from the perspective of priority: you cannot interject a spell or ability in the middle of it. You can only respond once the spell is fully cast and sitting on the stack (at which point priority is passed normally) or once the attackers/blockers have been fully and legally declared.

question: can you explain layers?
answer:
Yes — the layer system is the framework Magic uses to determine an object's final characteristics (power, toughness, color, types, abilities, etc.) when multiple continuous effects are trying to modify it at once.

How it works: per rule [613.1]/[613.1a], you start with the object's actual values (the printed characteristics for a card, or the defined values for a token/copy), and then apply all applicable continuous effects in a fixed sequence of layers:

- Layer 1: Rules and effects that modify copiable values [613.1a], which itself has sublayers — Layer 1a applies copy effects and merging with permanents [613.2a]/[730.1]. After layer 1 finishes, the object's characteristics are its 'copiable values' [613.2c].
- Layer 2: Control-changing effects (e.g., an effect like Act of Treason's 'gain control' clause, per [613.6]).
- Layer 3: Text-changing effects [613.1c].
- Layer 4: Type-changing effects (card type, subtype, supertype) [613.1d].
- Layer 5: Color-changing effects [613.1e].
- Layer 6: Ability-adding effects, keyword counters, ability-removing effects, and effects saying an object can't have an ability [613.1f].
- Layer 7: Power/toughness effects, which have their own sublayers [613.4a] — 7a is characteristic-defining abilities that set power/toughness (like Svogthos's ability referenced in [613.6]), 7b is effects that set power/toughness to a specific number, and 7c is effects that modify power/toughness (bonuses/penalties and counters), as shown in the Gray Ogre example in [613.5].

Within layers 2–6, characteristic-defining abilities are applied first, then everything else in timestamp order [613.3]. Within any layer or sublayer, effects are normally ordered by timestamp — earlier effects apply first [613.7] — unless a dependency exists, in which case dependency overrides timestamp order [613.8]/[613.8a]. An effect depends on another if it's in the same layer/sublayer, applying the other effect would change what the first effect does or applies to, and they aren't both (or split between) characteristic-defining abilities [613.8a].

Some effects span multiple layers at once (e.g., 'becomes the color of your choice and gets +1/+1' splits into layer 5 and layer 7c per [613.6]) — each part is applied in its own layer, and once an effect starts applying to a set of objects it keeps applying to that same set even if its source later disappears [613.6]. All of this happens continuously and automatically as the game state changes; the changes are instantaneous [613.5].

The worked examples in the rules illustrate this well: Honor of the Pure only pumps a creature while that creature is actually white, because layer 5 (color) is checked before layer 7c (the +1/+1 effect) applies or stops applying [613.5]. Similarly, Gray Ogre's power/toughness example shows counters, spell effects, and enchantments all stacking in layer 7c by timestamp, with a power/toughness-setting effect ('becomes 0/1') applying in layer 7b before the layer 7c modifiers are added on top [613.5].

question: how does the legend rule work?
answer:
The legend rule is a state-based action that checks whether a single player controls two or more legendary permanents with the exact same name. Legendary permanents are those with the supertype "legendary" [205.4d]. Whenever this happens, that player must choose one of those same-named legendary permanents to keep, and all the others are put into their owners' graveyards [704.5j] [Legend Rule].

Key points: 
- It only applies to permanents controlled by the SAME player. If two different players each control a legendary permanent with the same name, the legend rule doesn't apply to either of them—nothing happens.
- It's based on the permanents having the same name, not the same card. Two different printings of the same legendary card, or two tokens that happen to be given the same legendary name, still trigger the rule if controlled by the same player.
- It applies even to planeswalkers now: older planeswalker cards received errata to have the legendary supertype, so they're subject to the ordinary legend rule rather than the old, now-obsolete "planeswalker uniqueness rule" (which only checked for matching planeswalker types and was removed) [306.4] [Planeswalker Uniqueness Rule (Obsolete)].
- As a state-based action, the legend rule doesn't use the stack and can't be responded to [704.1]. It's checked automatically every time a player would receive priority—before that player actually gets priority—and this check-and-repeat process happens as many times as needed until no more state-based actions apply [117.5] [117.2d].
- The choice of which legendary permanent to keep is made by its controller and happens as part of the state-based action itself; there's no way for other players to intervene once the rule triggers, since state-based actions resolve immediately as a single event rather than going on the stack.

So in practice: if you ever end up controlling two permanents named, say, "Urza, Lord High Artificer," the game will immediately (next time state-based actions are checked) make you pick one to keep and send the other to your graveyard, with no opportunity for anyone to respond in between.

question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
answer:
Your creature is destroyed as a state-based action the next time the game checks for state-based actions, not the instant the damage is marked. Damage dealt to a creature never destroys it directly [120.5]; damage is just marked on it [120.3, 302.7], and then it's destroyed by a state-based action once total damage marked on it is greater than or equal to its toughness [704.5g, 120.6, 302.7].

State-based actions don't use the stack and aren't tied to any particular trigger event - they're checked every time a player would receive priority, before that player actually gets priority [704.3, 117.5, 405.6f, 117.2d]. So if damage is marked during the resolution of a spell or ability, the game doesn't check for lethal damage until that spell or ability finishes resolving; state-based actions ignore what happens mid-resolution [704.4]. Once the spell/ability is done resolving (or once combat damage is dealt in the combat damage step), the game checks state-based actions before anyone gets priority, and that's when your creature with lethal damage marked on it is destroyed [704.3, 510.3a].

Two timing notes depending on when you're asking about:
- If the damage was dealt as part of combat damage, the active player would normally get priority right after damage is dealt, but state-based actions (including this destruction) are checked first, so the creature dies before either player can act [510.3a, 704.3].
- If the damage was dealt mid-resolution of some other spell/ability's effect, destruction still waits until that resolution is completely finished and the game is about to hand out priority [704.4].

Special case - the cleanup step: normally no player gets priority during cleanup, and all damage is removed from permanents during that step anyway [514.2, 703.4p]. But if a creature already has lethal damage marked heading into that check, the state-based action fires before the damage is removed: the game checks for state-based actions first, performs them (destroying the creature), and only then removes damage/ends 'until end of turn' effects for what's left [514.3a, 514.2]. There are also rare effects that end the turn or end combat outright (e.g., Mandate of Peace ending combat); when that happens, the rules explicitly say state-based actions are checked as part of that process too, with no player getting priority and no triggers going on the stack in between [724.1c, 724.2c].

Bottom line: the creature isn't destroyed the moment damage equal to or exceeding its toughness is marked - it dies at the very next state-based action check, which happens automatically before any player would receive priority.

question: can I cast my commander from exile?
answer:
No — under the normal Commander rules, you cast your commander from the command zone, not from exile (rule 903.8: "A player may cast a commander they own from the command zone."). There is no rule granting permission to cast a commander directly out of exile.

However, if your commander card is currently sitting in exile, you have a path back into play. Rule 903.9a states: if a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and that card was put there since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may move it into the command zone — this is itself a state-based action (see 704.1, 704.6d). So the moment your commander lands in exile, you'll get the chance to relocate it to the command zone as a state-based action, and only then can you cast it from there under rule 903.8, paying the commander tax (an additional {2} for each previous time you've cast that commander from the command zone this game).

One caveat on timing: this only works if the commander was put into exile since the last state-based action check — i.e., it hasn't already been sitting there through a prior check where you declined (or weren't able) to move it. If you already passed on moving it to the command zone at an earlier check, rule 903.9a's window for that particular arrival in exile has closed, and the card just stays in exile unless some other effect intervenes.

So the practical answer: you can't cast it 'from exile' as such, but you can move it to the command zone via the state-based action in 903.9a and then cast it from there per 903.8.

question: what happens during the cleanup step?
answer: During the cleanup step (the second and final step of the ending phase), several things happen in this order: First, if the active player's hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven), they discard enough cards to get down to that number; this is a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [514.1]. Second, simultaneously, all damage marked on permanents (including phased-out permanents) is removed, and all 'until end of turn' and 'this turn' effects end; this also doesn't use the stack [514.2][703.4p]. Normally, no player receives priority during the cleanup step, so no spells can be cast and no abilities can be activated during it — it's one of the few steps (along with the untap step) where the step just ends once its specified actions are complete, rather than waiting for priority to pass [514.3][500.3]. However, there's an important exception: after the discard and the damage/effects cleanup, the game checks whether any state-based actions need to be performed (for example, a creature dying from the damage that was just removed wouldn't trigger this, but something like a creature having 0 toughness, or a triggered ability such as one that says 'at the beginning of the next cleanup step' would) or whether any triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack. If either is true, those state-based actions are performed, the triggered abilities go on the stack, and then the active player gets priority — players may cast spells and activate abilities normally. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, an entirely new cleanup step begins, repeating this whole process [514.3a][704.3]. If, on the other hand, that first check finds no state-based actions to perform and no triggered abilities waiting, then no player gets priority at all and the cleanup step simply ends [704.3]. This is a two-player-neutral rule — nothing about the cleanup step's procedure differs between a two-player game and a multiplayer game; the same discard-then-cleanup-then-conditional-priority sequence applies regardless of how many players are at the table.

question: when are state-based actions checked?
answer:
State-based actions (SBAs) are not checked on a fixed schedule tied to steps or phases — they're checked every time a player would receive priority, and they're dealt with before that player actually gets priority. Per rule [704.3] and [117.5], whenever a player would get priority, the game first checks the board for any of the SBA conditions and performs all applicable ones simultaneously as a single event; if any were performed, the check repeats, then any waiting triggered abilities are put on the stack, and the whole process repeats until a check produces no SBAs and no triggers are waiting — only then does the appropriate player actually get priority. Rule [704.2] confirms SBAs are checked continuously ('checked throughout the game') and aren't controlled by any player, and [117.2d]/[405.6f] both note SBAs don't use the stack and are dealt with before priority would be given.

There are two notable special cases:
- During the cleanup step, players normally don't get priority at all ([117.3a], [514.3a]). But the same check still happens: at the start of cleanup, the game checks whether any SBAs would be performed or any triggered abilities are waiting; if so, those SBAs are performed, the triggers go on the stack, and the active player gets priority ([514.3a], [704.3]). If nothing applies, no one gets priority and the step just ends.
- When an effect ends the combat phase or ends the turn (e.g., Mandate of Peace-style effects), the rules explicitly insert an SBA check as part of that resolution process even though no player gets priority and no triggers go on the stack at that moment ([724.2c], [724.1c]).

Separately, turn-based actions (like the draw step's draw, or discarding to hand size in the cleanup step under [514.1]) happen at the start/end of steps and phases and are distinct from SBAs — they're handled first, before SBAs are even checked for that priority pass ([703.3], [117.2c], [405.6e]).

This all applies regardless of how many players are in the game — nothing in these rules ties the SBA-checking process to a particular player count; it's simply tied to priority, which every player passes in and out of during their own turn or an opponent's turn in both two-player and multiplayer games.

question: how do I know who the active player is?
answer:
The active player is simply the player whose turn it currently is [102.1] [Active Player]. Every other player at the table is a nonactive player for that turn.

How this plays out depends on the format:

- In a normal (non-team) game, whether two-player or multiplayer, there is exactly one active player at any time: the person taking their turn. During that player's turn, they are the active player throughout all phases, and this carries through rules like priority passing to them first at the start of the upkeep, draw step, combat, and end step [504.2] [507.2] [509.2] [508.2] [510.3] [505.6].

- During the combat phase specifically, the active player is also the attacking player; in a two-player game the nonactive player is the defending player, while in multiplayer games where opponents don't all automatically become defending players, the active player must choose one opponent to be the defending player [506.2] [506.2b] [507.1].

- If the game uses the shared team turns option (mandatory in Two-Headed Giant and Archenemy), it's the team whose turn it is that is the active team, and every player on that team is simultaneously an active player [805.4a] [805.1]. When an ability refers to "the active player" in a shared-team-turns game, its controller chooses which one of the active team's players it refers to [805.9].

- Whenever multiple players must make a simultaneous choice or take a simultaneous action, the active player decides first, then the remaining players in turn order (Active Player, Nonactive Player order, or APNAP) [101.4] [101.4e] [Active Player, Nonactive Player Order]. In shared-team-turns games this is modified: the active team's players choose first (in any order among themselves), then each nonactive team in turn order [805.6].

So: for a standard two-player or multiplayer game without shared team turns, just look at whose turn it is — that's the active player. For Two-Headed Giant/Archenemy-style shared team turns, it's every player on the team whose turn it is.

This comes from rule [117.3c]: "If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward." Rule [601.2i] confirms this specifically for casting: once the steps of casting a spell are completed and it becomes cast, "if the spell's controller had priority before casting it, they get priority." The same logic applies to activating abilities and taking special actions, per [116.3].

The result is that each new spell you cast goes on top of the stack above the earlier ones, and they'll resolve in last-in-first-out order once everyone passes. This is generally called "holding priority."

This rule doesn't depend on how many players are in the game — it applies the same way whether you're in a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since [117.3c] simply says the player who had priority gets it back, regardless of table size. The only caveat is you must actually have had priority in the first place; if an opponent or another player currently holds priority, they act (and may respond) before you get another chance, and after any spell or ability resolves, priority reverts to the active player per [117.3b], not necessarily to you, unless you are the active player.

question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
answer:
Lore counters are added to Sagas as a turn-based action immediately after the active player's precombat main phase begins: that player puts a lore counter on each Saga enchantment they control that has one or more chapter abilities. This happens automatically and doesn't use the stack, so it can't be responded to.

Specifically, rule [703.4f] and [505.4] both describe this as a turn-based action tied to the start of the precombat main phase, and [714.3c] confirms this from the Saga rules themselves: "As a player's precombat main phase begins, that player puts a lore counter on each Saga they control with one or more chapter abilities. This turn-based action doesn't use the stack." (In an Archenemy game, per [703.4f], this happens after the archenemy's scheme action, though that's a special-format wrinkle rather than a change to the normal two-player or multiplayer timing.)

A couple of related nuances:
- Sagas without the read ahead keyword instead get their very first lore counter as a replacement effect when they enter the battlefield ([714.3a]: "This Saga enters with a lore counter on it"), not through this precombat main phase turn-based action. Sagas with read ahead similarly enter with a chosen number of lore counters via a replacement effect ([714.3b], [702.155b]). The precombat main phase turn-based action is what adds lore counters on every subsequent turn (and also applies to any Saga a player controls that didn't just enter, including ones gained through other means).
- After lore counters are placed, if a Saga's lore counter count is at least equal to its final chapter number, and it isn't currently the source of a chapter ability still on the stack, its controller sacrifices it as a state-based action ([714.4], [704.5s]).

This timing rule (start of precombat main phase) is the same regardless of how many players are in the game — nothing in the provided rules suggests turn order among more than two players changes when a player's own Sagas get their lore counters; it's simply tied to that player's own precombat main phase each turn.

question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
answer:
A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by an effect—generated when a spell or ability resolves, or when a replacement effect is applied—that will do something later in the game rather than immediately [Delayed Triggered Ability]. Like any triggered ability, its text contains "when," "whenever," or "at," though that word usually won't be the very first word of the ability [603.7, 603.7a].

Key points about how delayed triggered abilities work:

- They're created during the resolution of a spell or ability, as the result of a replacement effect being applied, or as the result of a static ability that lets a player take an action [603.7a]. A delayed triggered ability doesn't actually exist (and thus can't trigger) until it has been created, even if the event it watches for already happened just beforehand — for example, "When this creature leaves the battlefield" won't trigger if the creature already left before the ability was created [603.7a].

- Unless it has a stated duration (like "this turn"), a delayed triggered ability triggers only once, the next time its trigger event occurs. If that event happens more than once simultaneously, its controller chooses which occurrence causes it to trigger [603.7b].

- If it refers to a particular object, it still affects that object even if the object's characteristics change, but not if the object has left the zone it's expected to be in by the time the ability resolves (since an object that changes zones becomes a new object with no memory of its prior existence) [603.7c, 400.7].

- Its source and controller depend on what created it: a spell that creates one has that spell as its source and is controlled by whoever controlled the spell as it resolved [603.7d]; an activated or triggered ability that creates one uses that other ability's source, controlled by whoever controlled that ability as it resolved [603.7e]; a static ability generating a replacement effect that creates one has that permanent as the source, controlled by whoever controlled it when the replacement effect was applied [603.7f]; and similarly for static abilities that let a player take an action [603.7g].

- A special case, the "reflexive triggered ability" (rule 603.12), follows the same rules as delayed triggered abilities but is checked immediately upon creation, triggering based on whether its event already happened during the resolution of the ability that created it.

One-shot effects commonly use delayed triggered abilities to schedule an action for later, such as "exile this creature at the beginning of the next end step" [610.2].

question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
answer:
Yes. Instant and sorcery spells (i.e., non-permanent spells) absolutely can have abilities, and in fact several different kinds:

1. **Spell abilities** – The bulk of an instant or sorcery's rules text is a "spell ability," which is simply the set of instructions the spell's controller follows while that spell is resolving [113.3a]. This is the normal way instants/sorceries "do things."

2. **Static abilities** – An instant or sorcery can have a static ability, but per [113.6] such abilities "usually function only while that object is on the stack." Certain static abilities are explicit exceptions and can function even outside the stack: abilities that restrict/modify how the spell can be cast (e.g., additional-cost or alternative-cost text) work in any zone the spell could be cast from and also on the stack [113.6e, 604.5], and abilities phrased as "You may cast [this card]...," "You can't cast [this card]...," or "Cast [this card] only..." apply even while the card sits in hand (or another zone you could cast it from) [604.6]. Continuous effects from such static abilities can even grant a permanent spell an ability that lets it be cast [611.3d].

3. **Activated and triggered abilities** – An instant or sorcery card itself isn't limited to spell/static abilities; it can also have printed activated or triggered abilities. When such an ability is put on the stack, it becomes its own object distinct from the spell/card that created it, with only the text of that ability and no other characteristics [405.1, 405.4, 603.3, 113.1c]. These on-stack abilities aren't spells themselves, so they can't be countered by "counter target spell" effects, only by effects that specifically counter abilities [113.9].

So the short version: instants and sorceries commonly carry spell abilities that execute on resolution, and they can also carry static abilities (with the stack/hand-zone exceptions above) and activated/triggered abilities that go on the stack as separate objects when used.

This analysis doesn't depend on two-player vs. multiplayer distinctions — none of the cited rules vary by player count.

answer: Yes, you can activate mana abilities while a spell with split second is on the stack. None of this is overridden while a split-second spell sits on the stack, since split second's restriction text only names "spells" and "abilities that aren't mana abilities." This works the same whether it's a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since split second's restriction and the mana-ability exception aren't tied to player count.
